analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security benefits and pays for it with new taxes on income above $250,000 and on investment gains.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2025 with 42 House sponsors, the bill was referred to three committees and has had no committee or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise Social Security benefits across the board, increase benefits for the lowest-paid lifetime workers, use a cost-of-living formula that tracks what older people actually buy, and let children of deceased or disabled workers keep collecting benefits while in school until age 22. To pay for it, Social Security payroll taxes would apply to wages above $250,000 — today wages above $176,100 are exempt — and a tax on investment income would jump from 3.8% to 16.2%. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, especially lower earners. Every beneficiary would get a benefit increase through a richer benefit formula, and lifetime low earners would get a new minimum benefit pegged to the federal poverty line, rising with years worked up to 125% of poverty at 30 years. Benefits for everyone would grow faster under a cost-of-living index based on the spending of households over 62. Children of deceased or disabled workers who are full-time students could collect benefits until 22 instead of 19. Higher benefits and the merged trust fund would also extend the program's solvency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first factor in the benefit formula from 90% to 95% of average earnings and boosts the first bend point by 18%, increasing benefits for all beneficiaries starting in 2026.
Creates a new minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, scaled from 6.25% of the poverty guideline at 11 years of work up to 125% at 30 or more years.
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the CPI for Elderly Consumers, an index that reflects the spending patterns of older households, which typically face faster medical-cost inflation.
Extends child benefits to full-time students who are children of deceased or disabled workers until age 22, up from 19, and makes the same change under the Railroad Retirement Act.

Applies the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income between the current cap ($176,100 in 2025) and $250,000, and raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, extending it to active business income of high earners.
Merges the Old-Age and Survivors and Disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and investors. People earning wages above the current cap would pay payroll tax on income up to $250,000, with employers paying the matching share on those wages. Investors and high-income business owners would pay a 16.2% tax on net investment income — more than four times the current 3.8% rate — including on active business income that is currently exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, investors, and business owners

drawbacks.text: The tax on net investment income would rise from 3.8% to 16.2%, a more than fourfold increase that would fall on capital gains, dividends, and active business income of higher-income households, and critics argue such rates discourage investment and business formation.

Payroll tax would apply to earnings between the current cap and $250,000 without any corresponding increase in benefits for that income, meaning those earners pay more into the system without earning additional benefits.
The across-the-board and minimum-benefit increases permanently raise federal benefit obligations, and the bill's new revenues are dedicated to the trust fund rather than to deficit reduction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are broad and reach the people who rely on Social Security most — low earners, older households facing medical inflation, and students who lost a parent. The costs are concentrated on households with high wages and investment income. The main design question is the doughnut hole between the wage cap and $250,000, which taxes income without adding benefits, and the size of the investment-income tax increase. This is a large, deliberate redistribution toward ordinary beneficiaries, and it is honest about funding it rather than borrowing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late February 2025 and sent to three House committees, but no committee has acted on it and it has never come to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 27, 2025, joined by 19 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and also to the Education and Workforce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees; the Social Security provisions sit in Ways and Means.
It was also referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.
The bill has 41 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action has been taken since the February 2025 referrals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, high earners and investors, whose taxes remain unchanged, and opponents of expanding Social Security, since the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and opponents of expansion

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on February 27, 2025.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill's Social Security provisions sit in his committee; no markup or floor action has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; all 42 sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored.

industries.note: The tax on net investment income would rise from 3.8% to 16.2% and extend to active business income, substantially raising taxes on capital gains, dividends, and pass-through profits of higher-income households. Their gain from the status quo is the benefit expansion's lost funding.
Social Security payroll tax would apply to wages between the current $176,100 cap and $250,000, paid by both worker and employer. This income is currently exempt.
Employers would pay the matching payroll-tax share on employee wages above the current cap up to $250,000, a new cost on high-salary workforces.

industries.industry: Social Security beneficiaries and railroad workers' families
industries.note: Higher benefits, a stronger inflation index, a new minimum benefit, and student benefits until age 22 directly raise household income for retirees, disabled workers, and children of deceased or disabled workers.

analysis.trajectory: With Republican control of the House and Ways and Means, a bill raising payroll and investment taxes on high earners is very unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote this Congress. Similar Social Security expansion bills in past sessions died in committee. Unless the political balance shifts, it will sit without action until the session ends.
